title: Routing email automatically by purpose not topic
abstract: Presents large-scale extraction of pragmatic content from email using phrase-based speech-act detection and empirically observed speech-act patterns, evaluated on a corpus of 1,000 emails.

title: Task-Focused Summarization of Email
abstract: Describes task-focused email summarization that identifies action items and presents extracted tasks to users, supporting conversion of email content into to-do items.

title: Learning to Classify Email into “Speech Acts”
abstract: Introduces an email-act ontology combining communicative verbs such as request, propose, commit, and deliver with objects such as tasks, meetings, and information, and evaluates automatic classification of email into these acts. It is primarily message-level act detection rather than localized argument extraction.

title: Detecting Action-Items in E-mail
abstract: Detects emails that require action or response and, importantly, highlights the specific text expressing the request. The work explicitly contrasts localized action-item detection with whole-message text categorization.

title: On the collective classification of email "speech acts"
abstract: Classifies email messages for email acts such as requests and commitments and exploits sequential dependencies between messages in the same thread using collective classification. It provides useful evidence for contextual speech-act detection but remains primarily message-level classification.

title: Improving “Email Speech Acts” Analysis via N-gram Selection
abstract: Studies detection of email intents such as proposing a meeting and committing to a task, showing that contextual information, message preprocessing, and selected n-gram sequence features improve email-act classification.
venue: Analyzing Conversations in Text and Speech

title: Using Speech Acts to Categorize Email and Identify Email Genres
abstract: Defines email-oriented speech acts and uses them to characterize communicative purpose and email genres. The contribution is useful as an email speech-act taxonomy and act-detection baseline rather than as a slot extractor.

title: Can Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act be Reliably Identified in Email Messages?
abstract: Reports an exploratory annotation study in which human coders label the presence and strength of Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act in workplace email at sentence level. The study establishes empirical annotation evidence for distinguishing requests that impose action on recipients from promises by senders.

title: The nature of requests and commitments in email messages
abstract: Develops precise utterance-level definitions for requests and commitments in workplace email using speech-act theory and two annotation experiments on Enron email. It explicitly focuses on utterances that place responsibility for action on the sender or recipients and analyzes difficult surface realizations.

title: Requests and Commitments in Email are More Complex Than You Think: Eight Reasons to be Cautious
abstract: Analyzes difficult real-world cases encountered when annotating and extracting workplace-email requests and commitments, identifying eight categories of problematic phenomena and proposing annotation treatments. It is particularly relevant to conditional, repeated, ambiguous, and context-dependent action evidence.

title: Segmenting Email Message Text into Zones
abstract: Introduces Zebra, an SVM system that segments email bodies into functional zones using graphic, orthographic, and lexical cues. Although not an action extractor itself, the method helps localize current-message evidence and separate it from quoted replies, signatures, and other extraneous material.

title: Detecting Emails Containing Requests for Action
abstract: Detects email messages containing requests for action and improves classification by first segmenting messages into functional zones and restricting request detection to relevant content. The evaluated target is primarily message-level presence, so it is most useful as act-detection evidence rather than complete action-slot extraction.

title: Classifying Action Items for Semantic Email
abstract: Presents a rule-based system for recognizing email action items such as task assignments and meeting proposals. Its speech-act model structures action items with an Action, an Object, and where applicable a Subject or agent, and distinguishes actions including Request, Assign, Suggest, and Deliver.

title: Meeting Structure Annotation: Data and Tools
abstract: Presents annotations of hierarchical topic structure and action-item subdialogues over multi-party meeting corpora, together with representation and annotation tools. The action-item annotations provide source-grounded meeting data for studying how task assignment is established across multiple utterances.
venue: 6th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Detecting Action Items in Multi-party Meetings: Annotation and Initial Experiments
abstract: Defines action items as social actions involving a task description, timeframe, owner, and participant agreement, and introduces a hierarchical utterance-role annotation scheme for the assignment process. It investigates automatic detection while targeting extraction of information useful for reporting and summarization.
venue: Machine Learning for Multimodal Interaction, MLMI 2006

title: Shallow Discourse Structure for Action Item Detection
abstract: Uses shallow discourse structure and a hierarchical annotation scheme to detect action-item assignment regions in meeting transcripts. The work explicitly targets properties including responsible party, task, and deadline rather than treating an action item as an isolated sentence label.
venue: Analyzing Conversations in Text and Speech

title: Automatically Detecting Action Items in Audio Meeting Recordings
abstract: Uses a maximum-entropy model with lexical, temporal, syntactic, semantic, and prosodic features to identify action-item-related utterances in multi-party meeting recordings annotated for action items.
venue: 7th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Detecting and Summarizing Action Items in Multi-Party Dialogue
abstract: Detects subdialogues in which action items are proposed, discussed, and committed to, then uses semantic parsing to extract phrases that summarize the tasks involved. This directly supports source-grounded extraction rather than unconstrained action-item generation.
venue: 8th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Meeting Action Item Detection with Regularized Context Modeling
abstract: Introduces a manually annotated Chinese meeting corpus for action-item detection and a Context-Drop method that exploits local and global conversational context with contrastive learning. Experiments cover the new Chinese corpus and the English AMI corpus.

title: What Decisions Have You Made?: Automatic Decision Detection in Meeting Conversations
abstract: Studies automatic identification of decision-making dialogue acts in meeting conversations using lexical, prosodic, contextual, and topical evidence. It provides a communicative-decision counterpart to action-item detection.

title: Automatic Decision Detection in Meeting Speech
abstract: Presents the AMI DecisionDetector for locating decision-related dialogue acts and decision-related topic regions directly in complete meeting transcripts.
venue: Machine Learning for Multimodal Interaction, MLMI 2007

title: Modelling and Detecting Decisions in Multi-party Dialogue
abstract: Models multi-party decision making through dialogue acts with distinct roles in the decision process and investigates automatic detection of the resulting decision discussions.
venue: 9th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Real-time decision detection in multi-party dialogue
abstract: Automatically detects decision-making subdialogues in multi-party meetings in real time by distinguishing utterance types according to their roles in forming a decision.

title: Extracting Decisions from Multi-Party Dialogue Using Directed Graphical Models and Semantic Similarity
abstract: Uses directed graphical models to detect decision discussions and distinguishes dialogue-act roles such as the issue under discussion and its resolution. It also summarizes decisions by extracting phrases from the source dialogue rather than generating unsupported decisions.

title: Decision Detection Using Hierarchical Graphical Models
abstract: Uses hierarchical graphical models to represent dependencies among observed features, decision-related dialogue acts, and higher-level decision subdialogues for automatic detection of decisions in multi-party discussions.

title: The CALO Meeting Assistant System
abstract: Describes an end-to-end meeting understanding system whose semantic processing components include dialogue-act tagging, question-answer identification, action-item recognition, decision extraction, and summarization.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing

title: How to Do Things with Words
abstract: Foundational account of performative language and the distinction among locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts. It supplies the conceptual basis for later computational treatment of requests, promises, commitments, and other communicative actions.

title: Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language
abstract: Develops a systematic theory of speech acts and their constitutive rules, including acts such as requesting, ordering, promising, and asserting. It is conceptual background rather than empirical extraction evidence.

title: A classification of illocutionary acts
abstract: Proposes the influential illocutionary taxonomy of representatives, directives, commissives, expressives, and declarations. Directives and commissives provide the conceptual distinction underlying computational separation of requests from commitments.

title: Conversation Acts in Task-Oriented Spoken Dialogue
abstract: Extends traditional speech acts into fine-grained conversation acts covering grounding, turn-taking, and task-oriented joint action, and discusses how such acts can be recognized computationally.

title: Automatic Detection of Discourse Structure for Speech Recognition and Understanding
abstract: Introduces statistical detection of Switchboard discourse structure using a 42-class dialogue-act inventory and lexical, prosodic, and discourse-sequence information. The work is an important computational precursor for context-sensitive recognition of communicative acts.
venue: IEEE Workshop on Automatic Speech Recognition and Understanding

title: Dialogue act modeling for automatic tagging and recognition of conversational speech
abstract: Develops statistical dialogue-act tagging for conversational speech using lexical, prosodic, and discourse-sequence models. It provides transferable methods for modeling contextual dependencies among speech acts, including agreement and action-oriented dialogue functions.

title: SemEval-2010 Task 10: Linking Events and Their Participants in Discourse
abstract: Defines a discourse-level semantic-role task in which participants not locally expressed with an event predicate must be identified and linked to mentions elsewhere in the discourse. The task is directly transferable to recovering omitted owners or objects while preserving source evidence.
venue: Workshop on Semantic Evaluations: Recent Achievements and Future Directions

title: Semantic Role Labeling of Implicit Arguments for Nominal Predicates
abstract: Presents annotated data and discriminative methods for identifying implicit semantic arguments of nominal predicates and resolving them to discourse entities. The method is relevant to evidence-based recovery of omitted actors or objects but does not itself establish responsibility or commitment.

title: Combining Seemingly Incompatible Corpora for Implicit Semantic Role Labeling
abstract: Studies implicit semantic-role labeling across corpora with differing annotation schemes and shows how complementary resources can be combined for recovery of unexpressed arguments.
venue: Fourth Joint Conference on Lexical and Computational Semantics

title: Improving Implicit Semantic Role Labeling by Predicting Semantic Frame Arguments
abstract: Improves implicit semantic-role labeling by predicting semantic-frame arguments with a recurrent model and using those predictions to identify discourse-level fillers for missing roles.

title: Document-Level Event Argument Extraction by Conditional Generation
abstract: Formulates document-level event argument extraction as conditional generation from event templates and evaluates on WikiEvents. Its document-level reasoning over scattered and implicit participants is transferable to owner and object recovery, although speech-act status must be supplied separately.

title: Trigger is Not Sufficient: Exploiting Frame-aware Knowledge for Implicit Event Argument Extraction
abstract: Uses event-frame knowledge to improve extraction of implicit event arguments that are not recoverable from a trigger alone. The approach is transferable to omitted participant recovery but requires a separate communicative-act model to distinguish requested or committed actions from mere event mentions.

title: Agent-Specific Deontic Modality Detection in Legal Language
abstract: Introduces LEXDEMOD, which annotates deontic modality with respect to particular agents and includes modal-trigger spans. It distinguishes agent-specific normative meanings rather than collapsing obligation, permission, and related modalities, making it useful transfer evidence for responsibility and speech-act strength.

title: The Possible, the Plausible, and the Desirable: Event-Based Modality Detection for Language Processing
abstract: Models modality as a relation between modal expressions and the events they modify, covering a wider range of modal constructions than cue-only classification. The event-scoped representation is useful for distinguishing the status of an action rather than merely detecting a modal word.

title: The CoNLL-2010 Shared Task: Learning to Detect Hedges and their Scope in Natural Language Text
abstract: Defines evaluation for detecting hedge cues together with the textual scope affected by them. It is transferable to determining whether uncertainty actually scopes over an extracted action, though epistemic hedging alone does not establish a request or commitment.

title: *SEM 2012 Shared Task: Resolving the Scope and Focus of Negation
abstract: Defines shared tasks for identifying negation cues, their scope, and focus. Scope-sensitive negation is transferable to preventing negated actions from being incorrectly extracted as live requests, commitments, or decisions.

title: TimeML: Robust Specification of Event and Temporal Expressions in Text
abstract: Defines a markup language for events, temporal expressions, and temporal links that relate events to times and to other events. The event-time relation layer is directly relevant to linking a deadline expression to the action it constrains rather than extracting dates in isolation.

title: SemEval-2007 Task 15: TempEval Temporal Relation Identification
abstract: Defines benchmark tasks for identifying temporal relations involving events and temporal expressions, including event-time links. The relation component is transferable to associating a due date with the correct requested or committed action.

title: SemEval-2010 Task 13: TempEval-2
abstract: Extends TempEval evaluation to temporal expressions, events, and several classes of temporal relations, providing benchmark infrastructure for event-time linking rather than date recognition alone.

title: SemEval-2013 Task 1: TempEval-3: Evaluating Time Expressions, Events, and Temporal Relations
abstract: Evaluates extraction of temporal expressions and events together with temporal relations between them. The relation annotations provide transferable supervision for grounding deadlines and relative times to specific actions.

title: Temporal Anchoring of Events for the TimeBank Corpus
abstract: Studies temporal anchoring of events to explicit time expressions in TimeBank and provides methods and annotations for determining which time expression an event is anchored to.

title: Utilizing Relative Event Time to Enhance Event-Event Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Predicts relative event times and uses them to improve extraction of temporal relations between events. The approach is useful where deadline interpretation depends on event ordering or relative temporal anchors.

title: More than Classification: A Unified Framework for Event Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Represents event temporal relations through relations among event start and end time points rather than treating temporal-relation extraction as an opaque class label. This structured approach is transferable to reasoning about action deadlines and temporal constraints.
